NPT stands for National Pipe Thread, and is a taper thread that you typically would use with a sealant like Teflon paste or other. Not Teflon tape as a rule for us AN is an old Army Navy standard from ww2, and in this case Aviation refers to a 37 degree flared fitting in either gender. No sealant is used on AN flare fittings. With oil or fuel, It's very important you get these from a reliable source, the auto parts store may sell you an AN fitting, and it might even be 37 degree, but the quality is unknown and the possibility of mixing in a 45 degree fitting is there. You'd thread the NPT end into say a manifold or fuel valve tapped for pipe threads NPT then on the other end a 37 degree flared tubing with a "B" AN818 nut and AN 819 sleeve or you could put a hose on it with a female AN fitting. Make sense? Also pipe threads are measured on the i.d., tubing on the o.d., and hose size is based on 1 16" increments. So a 1 4" hose is 4'; 1 2" hose is 8 etc. Fuel pumps use an different O ring type fitting, when you get there don't try to thread a NPT thread into it. And finally most people insist on steel fittings on any fuel or oil lines in the engine compartment, a subject of some debate but I would, especially on the oil cooler. Vents lines Al fittings are ok, IMO. Hope this helps, I'm sure I missed something. Tim Andres All spelling errors are Apples responsibility. ! answer: The plans call for **3/8-inch-OD aluminum hard tubing, 0.035-inch wall, type 3003** for the fuel lines through the strakes and fuselage.[1][2] The **1/4-inch tubing is for vent lines**, not the fuel lines.[8]
